implementation_notes: Razor Pages is the pattern supplied by the framework: the @page directive turns a .cshtml file into an MVC action that handles requests directly, without going through a controller, its location under Pages/ defines the URL, and the paired PageModel class (same file name plus .cs) supplies one handler per verb - OnGet, OnPostAsync - which is where request handling, domain calls and view selection live. MapRazorPages() with endpoint routing replaces the classic dispatcher, and conventions, IPageFilter or [Authorize] on the PageModel replace the controller base class, so a hand-built controller hierarchy is unnecessary. MVC controller actions or minimal-API endpoints remain the right choice when a URL is an action inside a larger resource rather than a page.
pitfalls: Putting domain logic in OnGet/OnPost: the page model is the controller, not the service - it should orchestrate the workflow, not implement it.
A Razor Page handles only the verbs it has handlers for: a missing OnPost means a 405 (or a silently ignored form), not a fallback.
Authorisation must be attached per page ([Authorize] or a folder convention); nothing central enforces it, so a new page without it is publicly reachable.
